## Introduction

Engineering doctoral students represent the next generation of engineering faculty and are trained in the means and mechanisms of their technical discipline [1]. However, doctoral students often must embrace a multitude of roles during their tenure, including serving as research assistants, teaching assistants, employees, educators, and mentors, all in addition to and intersecting with their primary role as students [1]. As students, they are tasked with learning the professional and disciplinary norms, values, and practices of their research subfield, all the while undertaking significant intellectual labor to become a highly technical expert in their field [1]. As a result, doctoral students are highly embedded within a multitude of systems and power hierarchies in which they must navigate the complex, nuanced world of academia.

Minoritized doctoral students bring various additional identity- and marginality-based lenses that layer onto their lived experiences to their doctoral programs. Across engineering doctoral programs, minoritized doctoral students are severely underrepresented, have lower 7-year completion rates, and have higher 7-year attrition rates than non-minoritized doctoral students [2]. In addition, minoritized engineering students continue to face chilly climates, encounter microaggressions, and have lower senses of belonging and higher social isolation compared to their peers [3]–[6]. Previous work has shown how engineering institutions, such as doctoral programs, engineering academia, and engineering colleges, create and maintain systems that cause more negative experiences and lower outcomes for people with identities outside the able-bodied, cisgender, straight, white, male archetype of the typical engineering student [3]–[6]. Consistent with literature exploring institutions’ systemic impacts on minoritized students in engineering, we define these systems as systems of oppression, and their negative effects on minoritized students as marginalization [7]–[15]. While these negative experiences are detrimental to minoritized engineering students’ health and well-being [3], [4], [16], their lived experiences give minoritized doctoral students a unique perspective - one that enables them to viscerally understand and theorize about the inner mechanisms of the systems of oppression that bear on them as well as stand outside the engineering institution to critique it [7], [17], [18].

For some minoritized doctoral students, the picture of doctoral student responsibilities is complicated by their desire to engage in efforts to promote diversity, equity, inclusion, and social justice efforts in STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) disciplines [19].1

These students who choose to engage in such efforts must often take on additional intellectual, personal, emotional, and social labor that is often unseen or hidden in the eyes of the doctoral program. Additional labor may come in the form of the desire to be involved in outreach

These additional contributions often must be done on top of their doctoral student workload, incorporating another dimension and potential barrier into a highly rigorous and technical doctoral program. Thus, these minoritized engineering doctoral students exist in a particularly liminal space in which they straddle their technical engineering work with their social justice interest. The ways in which they navigate their doctoral program and encounter academic structures and institutions given these interests has not yet been significantly explored.

In this paper co-authored by two minoritized engineering doctoral students studying at a large private research university in the western United States, we utilize the critical framework and method of counterstory to give voice to our lived experiences inhabiting the liminal space between engineering and social justice. Through our narratives, we showcase how the additional labor we face due to our liminality extends beyond responsibilities: we constantly negotiate our roles within the engineering and social justice communities with institutional and academic gatekeepers who seek to regulate our lives in ways that reify and reproduce the power structures endemic to marginalization. By narrating our stories through an autoethnographic and critical lens, we seek to challenge and critique the unidimensional, one-track, progress-based nature of doctoral programs. In so doing, we hope to theorize and re-envision engineering doctoral programs as sites for social justice activism and systemic change within the engineering academy - particularly in motivating the future engineering professoriate to embrace social justice.

Counterstories: Lived Experiences, Criticality, and Resistance

Counterstory has a rich and varied history as an (auto)ethnographic method to foreground the lived experiences of marginalized people in academic research. First termed in 1989 by Richard Delgado, counterstories have been used in a variety of settings, particularly in Black and Latinx studies, to explore the holistic lived experiences of marginalized people confronting systemic oppression through narrative [20]–[22]. While various other methods have engaged similar types of narrative approaches, such as critical autoethnography [23], critical collaborative autoethnography [24], and narrative theory/inquiry [25], the key delineation between counterstories and other (auto)ethnographic or narrative methods is that counterstories seek to disrupt hegemonic, majoritarian narratives imposed by oppressive institutions - such as that the experiences of the able-bodied, cisgender straight white male engineering student apply to every student - by amplifying the voices of marginalized students [20], [23], [25]–[28]. Counterstories seek to not only illuminate and name the systems of oppression that impact marginalized people, but also highlight the ways they make meaning and theorize about their experiences in relation to dominant sources of power [24], [25], [27]. In writing and performing counterstories, marginalized communities create their own spaces to subvert dominant narratives imposed upon them by institutions and rewrite their experiences from their own perspectives [20], [26].

Underpinning the subversive nature and power of counterstories is the construct of criticality. Criticality, in this context, encompasses two components: first, as the “consideration of social inequities due to United States culture (e.g. sexism, racism)” [22] and second, as a


<!-- Page 4 -->


3

means and framework for “analyzing and challenging the stories of those in power and whose story is a natural part of dominant discourse” [26]. Emerging from critical race theory, criticality focuses on the deconstruction of systems of oppression by unpacking how people and institutions in power either actively or passively impose structural barriers to reproduce marginality and maintain the status quo. Criticality by itself is primarily an explanatory framework, enabling marginalized peoples to name and theorize about their lived experiences [25], [27]. However, the power of criticality lies in the ability for individuals to translate their theories, perspectives, and experiences of oppression into meaningful resistance praxis and calls to action [8], [9], [26], [27], [29]. It empowers marginalized people to supplant dominant narratives with their own, create spaces on the margins for themselves, and engage in liberatory activism to fight for social justice. In addition, drawing from its roots in critical race theory and queer Black feminist thought, criticality embraces intersectionality as a key construct in its framework, arguing that the systems of oppression for one group are intimately linked to those of another group and that one’s lived experiences are a unique product of their interlocking marginalized identities [7], [17], [27], [30]. Critiques of systemic oppression cannot occur categorically or in isolation but must take into account the layered, nuanced, messy interconnectedness of lived experiences as well as transcend identity boundaries. For individuals, criticality involves tying their lived experiences at the intersections of multiple privileged and non-privileged identities to broader oppressive social power hierarchies to move toward social justice and liberation. Thus, criticality embodies a key component of theorizing about oppression, narrating the lived experiences of marginalized peoples, empowering individuals to find personal agency to impart change within their spheres of influence, and uniting in solidarity behind larger collective resistance movements toward social justice.

In practice, criticality is employed through structural critiques of the engineering institution, often by marginalized people who inhabit academic engineering spaces. Previous work on engineering in social justice addresses the multitude of ways the engineering institution is oppressive, highlighting the myriads of interlocking social, professional, and institutional structures that cause marginalization [10]–[14], [31]. For example, Jennings constructed an anti-capitalist critique of the engineering institution, describing how curricular designs, interactions with employers, abusive professors, and more reinforced structural power hierarchies in engineering and forced Gender, Romantic, and Sexual Minority (GRSM) engineer participants out of the field [32]. Similarly, Riley, Slaton, and Pawley critique the extant state of engineering education’s approach to diversity by highlighting how diversity is often seen as “aspiring to solve the problem of underrepresentation or repair the leaky pipeline without deeply interrogating these structures” and call for social justice to be at the center of redesigned engineering institutions [14, p. 336]. These examples showcase how critical thought can be applied to social justice issues in engineering.

We define the process of expressing one’s experiences and critiques as critical theorizing. Critical theorizing is described by Secules drawing from bell hooks as the method through which marginalized individuals “make sense of their current situation as well as imagine new

4

possibilities. Theorizing is an interwoven process of understanding one’s situation in terms of existing oppressive social norms, questioning those norms, and eventually opening up our imagination to liberation from them” [13, p. 190]. bell hooks states, “theory emerges from the concrete, from my efforts to make sense of everyday life experiences” [33]. As Secules et al. notes from this passage, “hooks pushes back against the colonization of theory building as by and for academics, arguing for “democratic access to the process of theory-making” [25]. By providing a process and a forum to facilitate critical theorizing, counterstories embark on the democratic journey to restore voices to the marginalized people who write them, particularly in academic literature detailing their lived experiences. New mechanisms of historicized meaning-making can take place, and new modes of agency and resistance obscured by deficit-based or institutionalized perspectives can be uncovered through the narrative journey [23], [25], [34]. Moreover, these processes of narrating and theorizing and expressing can prove to be both personally healing and transformative for both participants and researchers, as mental, personal, and psychological barriers and traumas caused by systemic oppression are reckoned with in a safe space [25], [33]. Thus, critical theorizing is the process, and counterstories are the product, of a multifaceted movement toward illuminating and rectifying social injustices in engineering education with minoritized students at its center.

A key barrier to overcome for counterstories in the engineering education research space is the researcher-participant hierarchy. A salient critique of qualitative engineering education research is that the researcher-participant power dynamic significantly shapes how student experiences are presented in published research - primarily for the researcher’s personal and professional gain. Marginalized students must contribute their experiences to a person who may diminish their experiences or explain away or depersonalize their differences in experiences through analytical lenses. Qualitative researchers who seek to study the experiences of marginalized engineering students often report their findings in aggregate, synthesize information across participants, and craft narratives around participant data that meet the demands of an argument. The highly interactive process of data analysis filters out many of the raw experiences, emotions, and potential theorizing that students already have. In more recent literature, this has begun to be addressed through the constructs of positionality and reflexivity, where researchers seek to acknowledge the perspectives they bring to the work and how that may affect their analytical frames of reference [23], [35]–[38]. In addition, the rise of “me-search,” research on a marginalized population conducted by a member of the marginalized population, has sought to provide additional contextual basis for critically destabilizing the researcher-participant hierarchy and building rapport with marginalized students [28], [39], [40]. However, with the researcher continuing to pose as the middle-man between marginalized students and academic reporting of their lived experiences, the power hierarchy remains stable.

In this paper, we remove the barrier between academic/practitioner audiences and marginalized students by providing the raw, unfiltered counterstories of our participants - ourselves - as we encounter engineering doctoral programs actively hostile to our passions for social justice. We seek to challenge the researcher-participant hierarchy by sharing, theorizing,

We share our stories in the form of an academic research paper, partly because as doctoral students, that is what we do best, and partly because we recognize that the multitude of institutional structures that act upon us also serve to oppress us, silencing our vocal calls for social justice in engineering by devaluing our non-engineering work in technical engineering settings. In our counterstories, we seek to critique the engineering institutions that shape our doctoral program, illuminate how we have overcome barriers and found mechanisms of resistance through our work, and give perspectives to the challenges, doubts, and fears that lie ahead in our careers.

Methodological Approach and Research Quality

We came into this project wanting a way to tell stories of marginalization and oppression in a way and space that would be supportive and healthy. In our case, friendship and bonding over shared experiences were the prerequisites for us to become research partners. Friendship enabled us to understand each other deeper than if we were just labmates or colleagues; being friends translated to an ability to vocalize and interpret each other’s experiences through our own perspectives and create a shared safe space through which we could nurture our stories - which significantly impacted our research and counterstory writing process [24]. As Cann and Demeulenaere describe, friendship was a method in and of itself, a vehicle toward deeper, richer, co-constructed autoethnography in which our friendship enabled us to understand each other’s research process as well as each other better [24]. Thus, the narratives in this paper represent a co-construction of meaning: whereas the primary voice in each narrative is that of the individual, the counterstory itself was a product of a research process in which both individuals significantly shaped each other’s stories [24], [41].

Our conversations were never structured, and only after Jerry proposed that we formally write a paper on our conversations did we keep tabs on our research conversations. Formally, we only met twice during the latter half of 2021 and three times in early 2022 to discuss this research project; however, due to working in the same lab and running technical experiments together, we often had minor discussions about the project here and there. These informal discussions largely surrounded particular experiences that were salient to us at the time. Once we decided to write a paper, we had two “scoping conversations” - unstructured conversations surrounding our experiences in engineering that sought to elucidate common themes that both of us resonated with. During these meetings, we took extensive and detailed notes on our own and each other’s experiences, attempting to find resonances and commonalities in our narratives. We continually narrowed our scope of discussion until we felt that we had determined an aspect of our experiences that strongly encapsulated our collective lived experiences as doctoral students. That aspect turned out to be balance. Once we decided on the locus of balance and brainstormed various ways that our stories could tie together cohesively, we then parted ways to craft our counterstories. This enabled us to preserve the fidelity of our internal voices in our narratives

while still gaining perspective from each other. After writing our counterstories, we revised each other’s pieces for several iterations before writing this paper.

Throughout the process, we took into consideration several aspects of critical autoethnography. First, due to the nature and scope of the paper, we decided to dig deep into salient experiences that significantly impacted us and highlight particular overarching narratives rather than tell our life stories. This approach, focused on what Ellis, Adams, and Bochner calls “epiphanies,” allows us to focus our narratives on the most formative experiences in our lives rather than writing full-length autobiographies [42]. Consequently, we also negotiated through the many instances and moments that characterized our lived experiences, making difficult choices about what to include and what to leave out. Many of the pieces left out, such as our experiences related to identities in non-engineering spaces, form a significant part of who we are as people and shape our positionalities but bear less on our narratives than the dominant structures imposed on us by our doctoral programs.

Second, to ensure autoethnographic research quality, we considered Patton’s six criteria for autoethnographic research: reflexivity, substantial contribution, aesthetic merit, expression of a reality, impact, and relational ethics [43]. We discussed each of these constructs in detail while writing our counterstories and during the writing of the final paper. We incorporated reflexivity through our discussions and crafting of positionality statements after writing our counterstories, giving us an opportunity to understand precisely which frames of reference bore on our narratives. For substantial contribution and impact, we infused criticality as a fundamental tenet of our counterstories, paying particular attention to refining our critiques of systemic oppression in our narratives with the goal of highlighting the implications and potential approaches to rethinking social justice in engineering doctoral programs.. Toward aesthetic merit and expression of a reality, we narrated our stories in the first person, attempting our best to describe and evoke particular emotions we felt during the experiences to the best of our ability through our writing, tone, and style. Finally, we discussed the ways in which our friendship impacted our narratives and collaborative research and vice versa shaped this work, establishing relational ethics as the foundation for the research.

Third, we choose to refrain from contextualizing or analyzing our narratives beyond what is necessary to establish key background information for readers to understand our lived experiences. While analytical perspectives are important to the furthering of knowledge, they reify researcher perspectives and traditional means of knowledge production - a “researcher gaze” similar to the male gaze in feminist theory [44] - over the primary narrative and reinforce researcher-participant power dynamics. Consequently, the contextualization and analysis process introduces further interpretation in which authors are asked to retell their stories in light of previous literature, one that has often been riddled with examples of power dynamics and erasure of student voices in favor of deficit-based models [22]. Thus, we follow Solorzano and Bernal’s content approach by first presenting our counterstories in full without analysis before situating them within the broader engineering education field [26]. In structuring this paper, we start by first presenting our counterstories in full, then noting the commonalities we saw in each others’


<!-- Page 8 -->


7

narratives without the pretext of analysis in the discussion section. This enables readers to not only open the black box and peer through the window into our research process [45], but also bring their own lived experiences and interpretive frames to the work and draw their own conclusions based on the “data” we present in our institutional roles - not just as researchers, academics, and doctoral students, but fundamentally as people. We also present these stories with the recognition that some of our discourse may differ from and in fact conform to oppressive ideas. This is a product of our subjectivities, and we chose not to edit them to preserve the integrity of the counterstory in presenting the most well-aligned narratives to our thoughts and perceptions - messiness and contradictions are facts of life, and lived experiences are no different.

In the subsequent sections, we will first introduce the individual and shared contextual background to scaffold our lived experiences through our positionality statements, then move to the counterstories themselves. Finally, we conclude this paper with the connections we see with each other’s narratives in a co-written discussion section and invite the reader to co-construct their own interpretive knowledge, engage, and theorize with us on marginalized student experiences in engineering doctoral programs.

Positionalities Jerry

I came to this work because of my identities, background, and research interests. As a middle-class, cis-gender, able-bodied, Asian-American man and born and bred in the continental United States, the only identity that really made me stand out from my peers was my sexuality - and I often passed very much as straight. Our Shared Positionalities - Jerry & Crystal

When Jerry entered our engineering research lab, we became fast friends, brought together by our shared passion for social justice that seemed to not be reflected in anyone else in the group. Unlike the other students, who seemed to be religiously devoted to their technical engineering research, both of us led separate lives in the engineering social justice space, and both of us had encountered unexpected ways in which our social justice work intersected in our engineering experiences. Our conversations around social justice and experiences in the engineering doctoral program led naturally to this paper, an extension of our in-person conversations and storytelling experiences.

Counterstories Jerry - Navigating Academic Gatekeepers

When I was applying to PhD programs in electrical engineering, I wasn’t sure whether I was going to be able to continue doing my engineering education work. While I highly enjoyed the technical aspects of engineering, I had also found a significant passion for engineering education research, particularly in promoting social justice issues in my undergraduate studies. As a gay Asian-American engineering student, I was often in the racial and gender majority but in the sexual minority. In engineering, the people around me often didn’t talk about social justice issues and those who did primarily focused on race and binaristic gender identities, limiting their scope to what was clearly visible to the institution. Stepping outside the usual mantras of participating in “engineering outreach” and “diversity programming” into the more rigorous world of engineering education research enabled me to give voice to my critiques of the engineering education institution, particularly through the deconstructive lens of social justice. Social justice - as a way to expand the almost-cliche terms of “diversity” and “inclusion” beyond categorical identities and move toward critiquing oppressive institutions - was intimately intertwined with my education work, as it motivated me to do the engineering education research I wanted to do in a way that technical engineering did not, and in time, my work in this discipline became deeply connected with my personal identities and lived experiences.

To ensure that I could retain some aspect of that piece of my identity throughout my transition to graduate school, I made it a point to ask potential engineering faculty advisors their thoughts on social justice and DEI issues - in particular, what their stance would be if I pursued these interests academically. The responses were…interesting, to say the least. On average, they ranged from expressions that those issues were “for the younger generation to tackle” to “other people (not us) work on those issues”. By far the most common refrain was “as long as you produce good scientific research, what you do outside of the lab on your own time is not my business.” This wasn’t exactly an enthusiastic or even full support of my non-engineering, let alone social justice, interests, but at least it left the door open for me to live outside the lab and the purview of my eventual advisor.

The implication from those conversations was clear to me even before choosing a school and matriculating: if push ever came to shove during my PhD program, I had to remember that my electrical engineering degree had to come first. Not only was it the primary reason I was here, it was what would support me throughout my time at the university and give me access to all of its resources inside and outside my home department. Losing it would have far-reaching ramifications for me, including but not limited to, funding support and the inability to continue my research or even live in the area. As a graduate student, I could do both scientific research and social justice work, but without my scientific research, I would not be able to access the opportunities to do social justice work. This precarious realization that I had stumbled upon myself was constantly reinforced by none other than every graduate student I talked to as an incoming first-year. In their sage advice, only one person could make or break my experiences, goals, and career aspirations: an engineering advisor who supported me in both my engineering and social justice endeavors. Without a funding source for my engineering work, I would have no hope of being able to pursue my social justice research.

Luckily, the engineering advisor that I had scoped out during my application process turned out to be the best fit for me. We shared significant technical interests within the same broad subfields of novel semiconductor materials, and while his first priority was always his scientific research output, at least he cared enough about these issues to legitimize and entertain them when the time came. In my eyes, he was the best option of the few choices I had in the niche technical area I lived in. During our conversations, I was extremely upfront about my interest in DEI research in engineering, and I expressed in no uncertain terms that I was fully intending on incorporating some form of education research into my time at the university. With my hill and my goals firmly established, our conversations were productive, and he nominally supported my desire to pursue a second degree in education and do engineering education research - of course, conditional upon making “satisfactory academic progress” in my technical research, evaluated by him over time. After a certain amount of back-and-forth with respect to funding and degree progress timelines, he granted me his blessing to go forth and forge my path in both disciplines.

That was one half of the battle. Arguably the most important half, my advisor served as the primary gatekeeper to the engineering academic institution in which I must enter to make the change I want to make. The structures of the academic institution, where a PhD signifies extensive training and professionalization in the research methods and habits of an expert in the discipline, are the barriers that I faced. In straddling my interests, I was fortunate to have an advisor willing to support me financially and professionally in balancing my interests - with the clear caveat that my first priority was always to my engineering research. This conditional blessing was only given under the guise of “satisfactory academic progress,” whose evaluation was marked by my advisor’s whim. The latent implication was that he could withdraw his support at any time, and if I didn’t meet his standards for those who could solely focus on engineering, there could be consequences.

The other half of the battle was to be marginally easier: finding an advisor working in education whom I could use as a launchpad for my own social justice research. The main barrier was simply finding someone who was interested in engineering education - most education schools were already interested in social justice and STEM education as far as I could tell, but in my experience, engineering felt a little more niche than STEM. I had been fortunate in that my previous institution had one (single) professor who worked in engineering education already, but that was not guaranteed at every institution. As luck would have it, through a series of informal connections from my undergraduate engineering education advisor, I was able to connect with my current engineering education advisor as well as one of her former colleagues in the school of education. While it wouldn’t be the end of the world if it didn’t work out, I was determined to make something work.

When we finally met, I was pleasantly surprised by how supportive they were of having me conduct research and publish in two disciplines. Interestingly enough, they had had similar career trajectories, starting in engineering before jumping ship to embrace engineering education. Finding common ground in our experiences was easy, and having shared experiences of existing in both fields made it easier for me to be optimistic about potentially pursuing a degree in education concurrently with my doctorate in engineering. Furthermore, they were excited about my previous work and were interested in the various ideas I had come up with in terms of furthering social justice research in engineering education. Their enthusiasm in having me join their group meetings, actively participate in discussions, and talk about my previous work signaled their genuine interest in ensuring that I felt like I was being treated like a human being. I couldn’t help but notice the stark contrast between them and my engineering advisor, who merely saw the advisor-advisee relationship as employment and lab productivity with sprinkles of mentoring tossed in as an afterthought.

There was only one question that deterred them from giving their 100% full-fledged commitment to me, one that consistently came up not just in our initial conversations but in almost every step of the way as I sought to develop my own line of social justice-oriented research: Did my primary engineering advisor support me in what I was doing in the engineering education field? I always said yes since he did endorse my education work that one time, and I wasn’t about to jeopardize everything I’d worked for in engineering education research by asking him again. Attempting to reaffirm his commitment to my education work felt like walking on pins and needles - I wasn’t willing to risk him reneging on his initial promise by denying that I needed to produce more scientific research for him. It was certainly an uncomfortable question for me, as my engineering education advisors’ attentiveness to his whims made him an ever-present force even in the non-engineering work I did. That said, it wasn’t like they had much of a choice. At the end of the day, my engineering advisor was funding me, and he was the supervisor to the progress and completion of my primary degree. They recognized that their pull on my time was limited, my engineering advisor took precedence in the academic institution I inhabited, and therefore my scientific research came first in my priorities. As much as I would have loved to delve fully into engineering education for a few months with the option of

But at least I had now set myself up in a position to continue what I came into graduate school wanting to do: gain deep knowledge about two-dimensional semiconductor electronics while simultaneously working toward social justice in engineering education research.

Looking back as a PhD student halfway through their second year now, it took almost 1.5 years of graduate school and countless meetings with my advisors for me to be in a position where I felt secure enough in balancing my two disciplines to genuinely feel like I had a solid launchpad for my career interests. Much of this time was spent negotiating between my advisors, particularly my engineering advisor - they represented not only gatekeepers to the academic institution but also the particular norms and values I needed to learn to be accepted in the disciplinary academic circles I aspired to. After all, they were bound to the same institutional structures I was. Within these negotiations was the omniscience of the advisor-advisee power dynamic, invisible constraints surrounding me regardless of whether it was my engineering advisor constantly evaluating me on my (nominally informal) research updates for “satisfactory academic progress” or my engineering education advisors checking in periodically questioning whether my place in engineering was stable enough for me to maintain my extracurricular activities. In negotiating with my advisors, I saw a rehash of the individual confronting the institution, an institution that already prescribed what a PhD degree in electrical engineering demanded from its candidates and therefore regulated one’s work. But I, an individual with aspirations to reconceptualize the structure of the engineering education institution to uplift marginalized communities, wanted to take a different path, one that was far less traveled, one that would take me through both personal and intellectual fulfillment while furthering my career. By bargaining my time and prioritization of scientific projects over education ones, I was able to carve a path for me to achieve all of my goals and set myself up for a multidisciplinary education in graduate school. In doing so, I get the opportunity to produce rigorous, personally fulfilling social justice-oriented research that will hopefully make a difference in marginalized people’s lived experiences while at the same time increasing my depth and breadth of technical knowledge. While this negotiation is ongoing as I work on multiple scientific and education-related research projects at once, often switching between the two to optimize my time and productivity, my active resistance in defying the prescribed path for highly technical electrical engineering PhD students and engaging in social justice-oriented research aimed at deconstructing the engineering education institution has made me a better researcher, a better mentor, and a better person. My path forward is now clear - clear to continue straddling two almost completely separate disciplines with two diametrically opposed epistemologies for the time being in my PhD degree, drawing wisdom from both to inform my personal development. That is, until the next career decision comes along, and I am faced with renegotiating my boundaries again.

Crystal - Claiming Space & Disrupting Norms


<!-- Page 14 -->


13

I still remember the day I told my peers I had gotten accepted to Stanford for graduate school. I walked into the engineering honors society office excited to share the great news. My peers initially met me with all of the congratulations expected but then followed with many questions of my competence. They asked me if I could handle the program I had applied for, interviewed for, and got admitted for. Why was the simple fact that I was accepted not enough evidence that I deserved admission? None of my peers even applied to graduate school, yet they were suddenly experts on the admission process. They could not just accept my achievement at face value: that I had earned my spot at such an elite institution, one of the top institutions in the world for my discipline. They immediately questioned my merit whether I had what it took to complete the program before I even had the chance to prove it. The conversation eventually switched topics, and I left it at that since I did not want to further dwell on their negativity. While I think of myself as a self-confident and driven person, I still think about those comments to this day. Getting into Stanford for a Ph.D. program was a huge milestone and boosted my confidence in my ability as an academic, but at the same time, it brought new challenges. When I have a rough time with a problem set or an experiment isn’t going as I hoped, I wonder if my peers were right: was I good enough to be here?

A couple of months later, I started my graduate school journey a quarter early as an inaugural member of the Summer First program. This program was created by the School of Engineering Equity and Inclusion Initiative (EII) to give a jumpstart into graduate school for students who came from non-traditional academic backgrounds. It provided me with my first opportunity for community at Stanford, and I am still close to many of the graduate students I met in that program. Being able to acclimate to campus and learn all of the tools and lab norms early on helped me feel like I could be a successful graduate student. When I think back on that time, and how much my experience evolved from that point forward, I don’t think I would have stayed in graduate school without those early support systems established. Whenever I was having a hard time with my department cohort or others in the school of engineering, I had a solid group of administrators and fellow students who knew what I was going through and could remind me that I was not alone.

Unfortunately, once the fall quarter started, my rose-tinted glasses came off. I dealt with the everyday graduate struggles of balancing challenging coursework, unpredictable research timelines, and interpersonal issues, alongside the struggles of being a person of color in academia. I also dealt with isolation from peers after one of them assaulted me, being left out of academic discussions due to a perceived lack of competence, and microaggressions from others in the department. I constantly experienced microaggressions, constant stares as I walked through campus, a running pattern that reminded me of my “other” status. It quickly became a very hostile environment for me. For many people at Stanford, I drew attention because I did not fit the mold for what they consider a serious researcher to fit into. When it came time to make a study group for a big exam, I was not on their mind. Many of my peers never interacted with me despite taking the same coursework in undergrad. I didn’t look like I could help them or know anything, so I got passed over when it came time for a group project. I wanted to have a chance


<!-- Page 15 -->


14

to prove myself like everyone else instead of being assumed to be incompetent. Over the years, my coping mechanism automatically became that of working alone, never asking for help even when I struggled. I was trying to prove that I could do it alone and still do just as well as everyone else. Unfortunately, in a graduate school doctorate program, that is not the best path to take for long-term success. Researchers depend on each other for discovery. The collaboration of minds through idle conversation sparks the next great idea or breakthrough. Being the outsider within felt like a self-limiting problem that hindered my growth into the researcher I always wanted to become. I needed to find sanctuary away from these feelings.

So I did. I set out to change my environment by placing myself in spaces of diversity and inclusion. Shortly after, I signed up for the graduate recruitment team (organized by the EII team). When I went to my first conference recruiting for Stanford graduate admissions, I noticed that having someone like me at the table that had just gone through the admissions process and had shared identities with conference attendees seemed to lower their hesitancy to approach the booth. I spoke to many undergraduate students, and it reminded me of the importance of having diverse representation in higher education. That was when I decided to become the support system that others had been for me in my times of need. Once the pandemic hit, I was separated from many of my issues while on campus. Although I was no longer physically separated from my central support systems, I felt like I could no longer move towards helping future generations of graduate students. This feeling drove me to join the Black Engineering Graduate School Association (BEGSA). Since 2017, they have organized the Stanford Exposure to Research and Graduate Education (SERGE) program, which gives undergraduate students interested in applying to Stanford an opportunity to strengthen their graduate school applications and speak to professors they may be interested in working with. I got involved in planning both the 2020 and 2021 installments of the program – in 2020, it was able to go international for the first time since it was entirely virtual due to the pandemic. I think programs like SERGE reduce the intimidation barrier of applying to Stanford and increase confidence in students who might be experiencing imposter syndrome despite being very accomplished. Helping plan these events made me even more sure of my place in building up the next generation of underrepresented students doing innovative things in STEM.

For all the recruiting and mentorship work I have done for the School of Engineering, I was awarded the 2021 Justice, Equity, Diversity & Inclusion (JEDI) Service Graduation Award at my Master’s graduation. It was a huge surprise and great honor that made me appreciate all of the people at Stanford who set the example for me to give back to my community and inspire the next generation of graduate students. A considerable part of the reason I accomplished the things I have accomplished here is the inclusive spaces created for new students from non-traditional backgrounds coming to Stanford. While a diversity of thought is an important thing to strive for in academic spaces, our communities’ inclusion and equity efforts enable retention despite the hardships that often accompany graduate studies for minority students. Although being recognized for my work is a great honor, it came from a desire to validate my belonging and ensure that others like me didn’t have to experience what I went through. I sometimes worry if


<!-- Page 16 -->


15

the university uses the example of people like me - passionate graduate students who contribute their labor for free due to the goodness of their heart - as an excuse for not improving on their side. While there are many efforts to improve the culture of belonging in Stanford Engineering, I worry that there will be a point where the work seems finished when it is not, when administrators will become complacent in their roles and simply point to these programs without making actual change. In my opinion, it will take a lot more than just a few outreach programs here and there to fix a systemic issue as great as this. Institutionalized change must be led by paid administrators, not just ethically motivated graduate students working on incremental improvements to mitigate the negative effects of systemic oppression in their spare time.

## Discussion

When we look at our shared narratives of existing in the engineering space with minority identities, there are several common themes of the institution and those within it suppressing our full potential. When a student goes out of their way to take a path of pursuing social justice while also trying to explore a specialized topic of interest, this may not often be validated by peers and advisors. To ethically participate in research in an oppressive institution, we needed to seek other sources of reconciliation outside the engineering sphere. In Jerry’s counterstory, the engineering professors he encountered saw his social justice interests as extraneous in the best case and detrimental to productivity in the worst case. In Crystal’s counterstory, her interests in social justice deviated from the perceived norm of the dedicated researcher, which isolated her from her engineering peers and led her to turn elsewhere for support. This lack of support from within engineering led us to reach out to other communities' support and craft our support systems and environments outside of engineering.

In addition, the structures of our engineering doctoral programs do not allow us to live holistically as people. Everyday demands of graduate students are constructed to limit time for criticism and enhance technical research productivity instead of students’ personal best interests. For Jerry, the consideration of satisfactory academic progress linked tightly with technical research productivity - his social justice research interests hinge on his ability to continue producing at the same level as other graduate students who do not have the same interests. For Crystal, the microaggressions she faced were a symptom of a system that encouraged competition, which often meant avoiding those who engaged differently with the program or with technical research. Working together with someone perceived to be at a lower competence level would become a disadvantage for them, resulting in exclusion. The engineering doctoral program rewards those most committed to advancing technical research, placing intellectual advisors and peers as gatekeepers to success in the program. Even in publishing this paper together in an engineering education discipline, we considered whether our stories would be legitimized in a technical venue or contribute to our academic credentials in our program and marketability as future researchers.

Although we have been able to explore all of our social justice interests, we were still able to make it happen. Interested students are often required to put in the extra effort to seek out


<!-- Page 17 -->


16

relevant resources, which can be a difficult task at an institution as heterogeneously structured as Stanford. We recognize that we are special cases who have been able to work within our institution to meet our needs when other students may leave the program. We do not intend to speak for all minoritized graduate students in engineering; each graduate student’s experience is unique to their identities, and each individual interacts with their doctoral program in unique ways. In our narratives, we hope to illuminate some of the multitude of experiences of minoritized doctoral students to aid in guiding policy and practice for doctoral programs.

Many components of our experiences are not unique, and we find similar experiences for minoritized students across the engineering education literature. For example, our experiences highlight how microaggressions, tensions of hypervisibility and invisibility, and imposter syndrome have been integral components of our doctoral student experiences so far [46]–[51]. While it is a useful exercise to label the various forms of marginalization evident in our narratives, we transform our experiences as narrated in our counterstories into structural critiques of the engineering doctoral program we inhabit [14]. We find that the existing structures of our doctoral programs do not allow us to access our full academic and holistic potentials through engineering, and we use our counterstories to engage in acts of radical student agency and call for change within the engineering academic institution beyond simply reporting experiences [14]

From our counterstories, we provide a few recommendations for practitioners. First, simply providing safe spaces for students to discuss their needs with institutional representatives who do not inherently have power dynamics with the student would enable institutions to understand each individual’s needs and connect them with the appropriate resources. Second, practitioners should increase transparency and access to resources for students, particularly ensuring that students can readily access individually tailored resources provided by their program. This can help students feel more supported by the institution, which reduces burnout, improves mental health and well-being, and encourages research progress. Third, including and rewarding service and outreach components in doctoral programs incentivizes students to engage in social justice efforts and provides meaningful mechanisms of evaluation for social justice-engaged students’ additional workload compared to their peers. We call on practitioners and policymakers to find additional ways to incorporate social justice in their programs.

## Conclusion

Engineering doctoral students make up a portion of the rising generation of academics, professors, and industry leaders in engineering fields, yet minoritized doctoral students with interests in social justice may find themselves in a particularly unique and tenuous position. As Cann and DeMeulenare state,

“I can only afford to be a tourist in this academic solar system because my personal self is often not welcome; it is constantly in conflict with the professional space, particularly my research. I rarely discuss why I am so committed to racial justice in the educational system because it puts me at risk for being found out as too emotional, too personal, too close to the topic, too subjective. Even with a PhD, I continue to be at risk” [16, p. 152].


<!-- Page 18 -->


17

In this paper, we utilized the emergent critical method of counterstory to describe our experiences as two minoritized doctoral students in engineering navigating both the structures of our doctoral programs and the mechanisms through which we were allowed to explore social justice. We shed light on the systemic and structural inequities in our doctoral program that impacted our engagement with social justice issues, describing the additional burdens and responsibilities we had to willingly take on due to our social justice interests. While we were fortunate to have been able to strike this balance, the lack of resources and support from the department, the microaggressions and gatekeeping we encountered from peers and advisors, and the rigidity of our programs on valuing and expecting technical academic contributions over service work contributed significantly to our experiences in the liminal spaces of our programs. In our narratives, we question the values upon which doctoral programs are built and wonder how we can make structural change in doctoral programs that can be actively hostile to our non-technical, social justice-oriented interests. However, by critically reflecting on our experiences through narrative, we find agency in our social justice passions and strive to work toward improving our department - and the engineering academy - for the better.

## Internships’ Impact on Recognition for First-Generation and/or

## Low-Income Students

## Abstract

This qualitative research paper explores how internship experiences impact the recognition component of engineering professional identity for first-generation, low-income (FGLI) engineering students, drawing on the performance/competence, interest, and recognition (PCIR) framework. Technical experiences in internships are a crucial component of engineering internships, as they develop technical skill sets in real-world settings. However, the role of technical experiences in internships in developing recognition for FGLI students has not yet been explored. Ten FGLI students at a mid-size, private, highly-selective university in the United States participated in semi-structured interviews conducted through video-conferencing, of which six were selected for this paper due to their in-depth discussions on technical internships. After transcription, interview data were coded and analyzed using cluster matrix techniques that specifically targeted recognition-related codes. We found that participants who were assigned and supported in technical work felt recognized as an engineer by their colleagues and managers. The opposite was true when they were not assigned or supported in technical work. This work showcases that internships represent a highly contested locale in which recognition becomes the currency through which engineering professional identity could be cultivated or inhibited in FGLI students.

## Introduction

Engineering industry internships are widely considered to be an important pathway to gain entry to the engineering workforce. For engineering students who obtain internships, they are afforded a myriad of benefits, from real-world professional engineering experience and opportunities to explore various career paths to access to professional networks that would have otherwise been unattainable. In particular, minoritized students gain critical mastery experiences through engineering internships, which then increases their engineering self-efficacy and significantly guides their future engineering career decisions [1]–[3]. However, internship experiences are not equally accessed by all undergraduate engineering students [4], as it is firmly established that minoritized students may encounter institutional barriers to career resources and be stymied in their professional careers by structural inequities, leading to lower senses of belonging and uncertain professional identities [5]–[7]. In particular, within engineering, first-generation and/or low-income (FGLI) students encounter knowledge practices that devalue and delegitimize their own experiences, financial pressures, curriculum overload, lower family support that may contribute to accessing engineering internships [6], [7].


<!-- Page 3 -->


This qualitative research paper seeks to investigate the role(s) engineering industry internships play in developing engineering professional identity for FGLI students. We ask the question, “How do technical engineering industry internship experiences impact FGLI students’ recognition and engineering professional identities?” Interviews with ten self-identifying FGLI engineering students at a mid-size private university were conducted and analyzed through the lens of recognition, and six participants were selected for this paper to highlight their technical experiences [8], [9]. We find that technical projects in internships make a significant impact on recognition, thereby either increasing or decreasing students’ engineering professional identities.

Theoretical Framework

This study seeks to deepen knowledge related to the Performance/Competence, Interest, Recognition (PCIR) framework of engineering professional identity (EPI) by explicitly elucidating recognition during internship experiences as a key influence on FGLI students. In the PCIR model, the construct of recognition is defined as how others perceive a particular individual, in this case, an engineering student, as an engineer [8]. Particularly, Scalaro et al. define meaningful recognition as recognition that increases, maintains, and/or sustains an engineering student’s engineering identity that comes from meaningful external sources to the student, such as peers, mentors, and family [9]. For this paper, we adopt Scalaro et al.’s definition of meaningful recognition as our primary definition of recognition.

As internships are a way for engineering students to gain additional real-world, hands-on practical experience prior to entering the engineering workforce, technical work is a cornerstone for engineering internship experiences [1], [2]. ## Methods

Study Site and Participants

Ten FGLI students at a mid-size, private, highly-selective university in the United States, participated in semi-structured interviews conducted through video-conferencing. Participants were recruited through an online pre-screening survey that was distributed through engineering


<!-- Page 4 -->


departmental and student organization listservs. The pre-screening survey requested survey respondents to list the number of engineering industry internship experiences and the top three most memorable internships. In addition, the survey collected demographic information to determine the respondent’s FGLI status. Respondents who completed the pre-screening survey were notified that, if selected for a follow-up interview, they would be reimbursed with a $25 gift card for their time. The study was approved by both collaborating institutions’ institutional review boards.

Eligible interview participants were selected based on the number of internships they had and their first-generation and/or low-income status. Eligible interviewees needed to have completed at least one engineering industry internship to be interviewed; students who tried but did not get internships were excluded from the sample. We used items on the pre-screening survey for participant selection purposes. We defined “first-generation” as students who self-identified up to two “parents” (who included parents, stepparents, grandparents, guardians, or other), neither of whom was reported as having graduated with a Bachelor’s degree or higher. We defined “low-income” as students who answered “low-income” or “lower-middle income” to an item asking them to self-report how they would describe their family when they were growing up. Details on the evolution of these items and definitions of first-generation and low-income are discussed at length elsewhere [4], [12]. Eligible interviewees were contacted through university email to arrange the logistics of the interview. Twelve students were selected from the survey respondent pool, and ten students were interviewed. Two students did not respond to the follow-up interview request.

In this paper, we focus on the six interviewees who discussed their technical work contributions to their internships in the greatest depth. Table 1 shows the demographics of the six interview participants. Five participants identified as men, and one identified as a woman. Since Asian and Asian-American students are overrepresented in engineering compared to the United States national population, they are considered a majority group in our study [13]. Three participants identified as Hispanic or Latinx, two as Asian or Asian-American, and one as Black or African-American.

Data Collection

The first author conducted semi-structured 45-minute interviews with each of the participants virtually over Zoom. These interviews were both video- and audio-recorded, and the audio recording was transcribed by an online transcription service. The video data was not used in the analysis. After the interview, participants were reimbursed with a $25 Amazon gift card. Semi-structured interviews were chosen as the primary qualitative method for this study to enable interviewers to ask probing questions based on the interviewee’s response, encouraging elaboration and deeper elicitation of experiences [14]. Questions ranged from participants’


<!-- Page 5 -->


overall experiences in their internships to specific instances of meaningful perceived recognition before, during, and after their internships.

Data Analysis

After transcription, the transcripts were cleaned and prepared for data analysis in the qualitative coding software Dedoose. Three authors participated in the data analysis and coding. All coders did an initial reading of the transcripts. Based on this initial read and the research questions, an initial codebook was generated using both deductive and inductive codes through discussion between the three coders and prior literature on FGLI students [5], [6], [15]. One transcript was selected as a “norming” transcript, and all coders used the initial codebook to code the transcript. Discrepancies were discussed until a consensus was reached, and the initial codebook was adjusted for coding. To maintain inter-rater reliability and incorporate trustworthiness into the coding process, negative cases were collectively identified for each code from the transcripts. The interviews were then divided so that each coder coded six transcripts, and each transcript saw two coders. After coding, the three coders individually wrote an analytical memo on the subset of transcripts they coded. The three coders consolidated the codes into findings, ensuring consensus on all findings. For this paper, we discuss our findings related to participants’ perceived recognition as an engineer by others.


<!-- Page 6 -->


Trustworthiness & Positionality

In qualitative research, trustworthiness is a key component of ensuring data quality, validation and reliability throughout the research process. This ensures that participants’ experiences and narratives are represented accurately, are situated within their particular contexts, and are presented clearly through the interpretive lenses of the researchers [16]–[19]. In our study, we undertook several methods to ensure trustworthiness: purposive sampling, negative case analysis, and reflexivity. Purposive sampling ensures that the study participants accurately reflect and represent the target population of study. In our interview selection process, we excluded candidates who were not either first-generation or low-income, ensuring that all interviewees were members of the target study population. Negative case analysis increases the precision of the codebook by anticipating potential discrepancies in the coding process and refines the coding process by providing comparative references for which excerpts belong and do not belong to a certain code [20]. During the development of the codebook, at least one negative case was identified for each code. Reflexivity is the acknowledgement that the researchers enact significant influence on the research process simply by being the active researcher [19], [21]. Analytical memoing enables researchers to reflect on how they influence the data and how their personal views impact their interpretations of the data [22]. The coding team wrote analytical memos after coding and prior to discussing and consolidating codes into findings and carefully considered their positionalities in the work.

The research team also intentionally and explicitly discussed their positionality throughout the research process [17], [18], [23]. Positionality asks researchers to consider the ways in which the researchers’ identities directly and indirectly affect the research process, from epistemological background to research generation to data analysis and reporting [17]. We leveraged our individual positionality to assign roles and to enrich discussions about the themes emerging from the data. For example, the graduate student on our research team interviewed the participants to mitigate power dynamics, and used his experiences being at the same institution to connect with participants and build rapport [14]. One member of the research team, who holds a position at a separate institution, recruited the participants to minimize perceived coercion. Our research team brought into the data analysis and discussion of findings identification with marginalized identitities including gay, Asian-American, Black, female, and first-generation college student. Several members of the research team have engaged in prior engineering education work with marginalized identities.

Findings

Technical work was a cornerstone of how participants viewed their engineering internships. Highly technical internships in which participants engaged in technical tasks showcased to them that they were being recognized as engineers and entrusted with the


<!-- Page 7 -->


responsibilities that came with the title. Inversely, internships that focused on “busy work” gave participants the perception that companies and their representatives did not recognize them as engineers, devaluing and delegitimizing their engineering skill sets. As a result, participants’ engineering professional identities were affected by technical and non-technical internship work assignments.  In this section, we present participant perspectives highlighting how FGLI students navigated the technical work aspect of internships.

Successfully engaging in tasks the participants viewed as ‘engineering work’ was cited by three participants as enhancing their recognition. This work was almost exclusively technical in nature. Aspen related,

“I think that [company] was the first time that people looked at me as an engineer. So I was given engineering work to do. I was doing testing, I was troubleshooting machines. Yeah. Right now I'm in a project that I've been troubleshooting a machine for a month. A lot of electrical parts broke and some mechanical parts broke. And it's nice to be seen like that.”

In addition to the tasks Aspen named specifically, testing and troubleshooting, Kai noted the skills he gained through his internship as key takeaways, stating that after his experience,  “I can read through the datasheet, take out what I want. I can call the manufacturer and talk about inductances with this engineer from [other company].” Lex similarly noted, “I was able to do everything from prototyping to mass production and a lot of parts and be a DRI, a directly responsible individual, on a lot of projects.” Participants recognized both their own competence (“I can…” and “I was able to…” and “I was doing…”), as well as how others viewed them as a result of their competence, such as when Aspen says “the first time that people looked at me as an engineer… it’s nice to be seen like that.” Lex had a particularly powerful experience at his internships, as after interning for his company for a year and taking on so much responsibility, his coworkers were surprised to learn that he was just an intern and was returning back to school. This implicit form of recognition, made explicit only at the end of the internship, increased his perceived engineering professional identity.

Several participants also defined their enhanced recognition in relation to their evolution beyond engineering student tasks. Kai mentioned after performing certain technical tasks, “it's the first time I felt like a professional engineer and not just an engineering student. That's a very, very nice, fulfilling moment. It's like, ‘Yes, all right. I think I'm doing this engineering thing right.’ Similarly, Lex noted this evolution “I think I saw myself as an engineering student who knew a lot of the concepts, but had no real world experience…. And I think that the year-long experience at [company], since I was able to do everything from [list of technical tasks] did help me feel more like an engineer.” While in these cases, participants were describing a shift in how they felt about themselves rather than strictly how others see them, they were key moments in


<!-- Page 8 -->


participants’ internship experiences that were invaluable in their engineering professional identity development.

The most common event that diminished a participant’s recognition during the internship was being asked to complete tasks that they did not consider to be engineering work or did not consider to be impactful (“busy work,” as some participants colloquially called it). Three participants reported being given non-technical or non-engineering work, which they attributed to their supervisors and companies not valuing them. Ari defined this work in terms of what it was not: “I think, personally, for me, I think I would have seen myself as more of an engineer if I had done research and stuff. I feel like, to me, that's engineering: doing tests, hands-on designing, building, creating things.” Skylar explicitly highlighted office administration-type tasks as not engineering work:

“Oh, I know my very first internship, the one after my freshman year, one of the things I did for a few weeks was photocopying a bunch of textbooks and binder papers, and it wasn't the most exciting thing ever, especially since my internship was supposed to be an engineering internship. And part of the reason why I chose that internship was because it was supposed to be an engineering internship [emphasis added], as opposed to, one of the other local companies had more a finance-type position for me, but I really wanted the engineering experience and I didn't know exactly that I'd be stuck doing what I was doing.”

Moreover, the three participants with diminished recognition emphasized that their internship tasks were not going to have an impact on the company. For Marc, this meant not being challenged: “I think it relates back to the theme of me not working in exactly the toughest projects or kind of mundane projects.” Lex, along with others, described this as busy work,

“they were kind of BS tasks, but they were like, "Design this," but we weren't even going to use it. It's just so that you get a practice with tolerance analysis and all this. And so a lot of those tasks felt like it was just busy work. And just for me to learn stuff, even though it's not going to be used. And so that very much did make me feel like I'm not really part of the team. They're just keeping me busy.”

The three participants further considered tasks that diminished their recognition as those not related to coursework from their engineering curricula. Ari related, “I wasn't really using any of the things I learned in college or ... Yeah. It was very like, ‘Oh, is this what industry looks like?’ Or, ‘Am I even really an engineer if I'm not building stuff or designing things?’” Aspen had a particular experience where she was discouraged from tasks that would have used her mechanical engineering coursework, stating, “I'm a mechanical engineering student, I do tractions and things like that. So for example, my job at [company], they had some tests to do on


<!-- Page 9 -->


statics and et cetera and then the guy saw that I was a product designer and he was like, you don't need to do this. We're going to just talk about the colors in the airplane and things like that.” She contrasted this with a later internship that enhanced her engineering recognition where “I have the basis of the mechanical engineering department, I just do a lot of other stuff. I think that [company] was the first time that people looked at me as an engineer. So I was given engineering work to do.” For these FGLI participants, busy work represented the clear communication that they were not recognized as engineers - their skills were being undervalued, underutilized, and delegitimized in their industry positions.

Technical work was a foundation for engineering internship experiences, particularly since participants sought them as a primary way to increase their engineering knowledge and technical skill sets and gain real-world practical experience outside the classroom. For those who were able to have those experiences, the recognition of them as engineers by their companies increased their engineering professional identities, and for those whose internships were simply busy work, the lack of recognition of them as engineers caused their engineering professional identity to suffer.

## Discussion

The career-propelling benefits of engineering internships have been well-documented [1], [2]. However, in our findings, not all internships were positive experiences for participants. While all internships provide invaluable learning experiences to participants, technical and non-technical work assignments affected participants’ engineering professional identities. Positive technical experiences gave participants the well-documented benefits of internships, such as real-world experience, professional networking opportunities, and positive recognition experiences, boosting their engineering professional identities. In contrast, negative experiences that amounted to busy work or non-technical tasks indicated little to no recognition of students’ value in the engineering workplace, reducing engineering professional identity. Both positive and negative experiences served as opportunities for learning and reflection for FGLI participants, but the benefits for developing technical skills and engineering identity were not experienced equally.

Implications

This work has implications for engineering education stakeholders who interact with students engaging in internships. An affirming internship experience that enhances an FGLI student’s recognition may help motivate and retain individuals in their final years of the engineering curriculum and help launch these students into full-time jobs in the engineering and technology workforce.


<!-- Page 10 -->


Our analysis points to concrete actions that companies can take to address aspects of their internship experiences related to enhancing recognition. Managers of interns should critically consider the type of work interns are performing and ensure that it is technical, challenging, and impactful. Training and carefully assigning mentors and/or supervisors that will support interns in performing and achieving success in the technical aspects of their work is also important.

For both companies and institutions, asking and listening to FGLI students about their internship experiences in explicit conversations will aid in centering the importance of the internship experience in the engineering and technology field and guide directions for policy making within the unique context of each university, department, and company. It is important to listen to these conversations in good faith, as marginalized students have different experiences with internships and career trajectories compared to other students as a result of their identities. Understanding their struggles and proposed solutions straight from the source will enable action that directly impacts them and responds to their concerns.

Limitations and Future Work

This qualitative study aimed to address how internships impact recognition for engineering students near or at the end of their careers as students. The findings in our study may not be generalizable for several reasons. Since our study was conducted during the pandemic, internship experiences related to recognition could have varied in part because of the restrictions of COVID. Online versus in-person experiences could have/did influence engagement and relationships between students and their employers. As a result, projects given to the intern, project scope, and how the projects were evaluated could have been affected. Future work should evaluate whether and what significant differences there are between online/virtual and in-person internships and their impacts on FGLI students versus non-FGLI students.

Additionally, study population size and demographics could affect the broad applicability of our findings. Due to the nature and scope of the paper, we focused our analysis on FGLI student experiences but did not include non-FGLI students or students who were not able to obtain internships during their undergraduate engineering career. This makes comparisons difficult across various groups of students in engineering. Future work should seek to compare experiences to further deepen our understanding of other, possibly marginalized, students with different identities. Only mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, and product design students were captured in our sample. Future work should investigate FGLI student internship experiences in other engineering disciplines, as different perspectives on the nature and value of engineering internship work may vary.

Finally, the experiences of FGLI engineering students are highly multidimensional, and internships represent only one area of FGLI student experiences. Future work should focus on


<!-- Page 11 -->


exploring the barriers and supports encountered by FGLI students as well as how they may bring unique forms of knowledge to engineering internships that are not always validated or legitimized by the status quo of the engineering institution. In addition, internships are a unique intersection between technical and interpersonal interactions, as internships often require highly social activities such as communication between coworkers, peers, and mentors. How this comes to bear on FGLI students should be further explicated. These perspectives will be explored in future papers by the authors.

## Conclusion

Internships yielded a significant impact on FGLI students in developing technical skills and their engineering professional identity. By focusing on recognition, one pillar of the PCIR engineering professional identity model [8], [9], we showcase that internships represent a highly contested locale in which recognition becomes the currency through which engineering professional identity could be cultivated or inhibited in FGLI students. This work substantially adds to the continuing dialogue and evolving literature on both internships and FGLI student experiences, highlighting that internships continue to be a powerful mechanism for driving the career paths for future engineers with marginalized backgrounds.
